summary: Documents issues and potential problems raised against proposals that let one subnet span multiple links connected by routers. It lists the concerns for readers who might consider such a design. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4903 explains why a subnet that crosses routed links can break software and protocols that expect subnet traffic to remain on one link. It describes the main compatibility and security problems and recommends link models that preserve existing IP assumptions.

subtitle: Why assigning one subnet across multiple routed links conflicts with common IP assumptions.

tldr.problem: Some proposals let one IP subnet span multiple links joined by routers, changing the established relationship between a subnet and a link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes problems for TTL and Hop Limit assumptions, link-scoped multicast and broadcast, duplicate address detection, and security mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The memo recommends avoiding multi-link subnets and using multi-access or point-to-point link models. NBMA is an option for cases that do not need multicast or broadcast.

today: RFC 4903 is Informational and was published in June 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Existing Subnet Model
sections.content:
When networks grew beyond one cable, designers could assign a separate network number to each cable, use transparent subnets, or divide one network number into subnets. The IETF standardized explicit subnetting, in which hosts learn a subnet mask.

IPv4 and IPv6 associate a subnet prefix with one link, although multiple subnet prefixes may share a link. A proposal to extend one subnet across links connected by routers would change this model. The IPv6 working group abandoned the proposals described here after considering the issues in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP model associates each subnet with one link. A design that stretches a subnet across routed links changes that assumption.

sections.title: TTL and Hop Limit Assumptions
sections.content:
A link is bounded by routers that reduce IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit when forwarding packets. Some applications send packets with a value of 1 to keep them on a link. Other protocols check for a value of 255 on receipt to reject packets from off-link senders.

If a subnet spans routed links, these mechanisms no longer line up with the subnet boundary. The RFC cites Neighbor Discovery as a protocol that checks a received Hop Limit of 255. Applications may also assume that TTL or Hop Limit 1 confines traffic to the local subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers reduce TTL or Hop Limit as packets cross links. Protocols that use these values to identify local traffic can fail when one subnet spans more than one link.

sections.title: Multicast, Broadcast, and Address Detection
sections.content:
Routers generally do not forward link-scoped multicast or broadcast traffic. Neighbor Discovery, DHCP, routing protocols, and service-discovery protocols may depend on messages that stay within one link. Without protocol-specific proxying, these messages do not reach nodes on another link in the same proposed subnet.

Duplicate Address Detection also uses link-scoped multicast or broadcast. If a device checks a link-local address for uniqueness and assumes the same interface identifier is unique across multiple links, duplicate addresses can result. The RFC notes that proxying an arbitrary number of protocols does not scale.
sections.plainLanguage: Many protocols send local messages that routers do not forward. A multi-link subnet can separate devices that those messages need to reach.

sections.title: Security and Recommended Link Models
sections.content:
Security protocols that assume a subnet is one link may fail across a multi-link subnet. SEND protects Neighbor Discovery messages containing link-layer addresses, which differ at each routed link. TTL or Hop Limit checks of 255 that help reject off-link spoofing also depend on a single-link boundary.

The IAB recommends the multi-access link model or point-to-point link model. An NBMA variant has no broadcast or multicast, so protocols that require those functions will not work. The RFC says multi-link subnet designs should be avoided and existing designs should investigate moving to one of the other models.
sections.plainLanguage: A multi-link subnet can weaken security checks that depend on a single link. The RFC recommends multi-access or point-to-point links instead.
